title: The Refugee Who Invented Ottoman Printing
event_summary: In early 1493, David and Samuel ibn Nahmias, Sephardic Jews expelled from Spain during the Alhambra Decree of 1492, established the first printing press in the Ottoman Empire in Constantinople. Using Hebrew type they had carried across the Mediterranean, they printed the Arba'ah Turim, a comprehensive Jewish legal code, making it one of the earliest printed books in the Islamic world. Sultan Bayezid II, who had actively welcomed Iberian Jewish refugees, permitted the press to operate freely as long as it did not print in Arabic or Turkish script.
why_forgotten: The event falls between two much more famous narratives — Gutenberg's press in 1450s Europe and the Ottoman ban on Arabic-script printing that lasted until 1729 — so it gets lost in the gap. Ottoman historiography often emphasizes the later Ibrahim Müteferrika press as the empire's printing origin, while European histories credit printing's spread solely to Western networks. The specifically Jewish and refugee dimension of the story fits uncomfortably into nationalist narratives on all sides.
why_it_matters: The Nahmias press demonstrated that technology transfer often follows refugee routes rather than trade routes — a pattern repeated with Huguenot craftsmen, German-Jewish scientists, and Syrian engineers today. It created a Sephardic intellectual infrastructure across the Ottoman world that preserved and disseminated philosophical and scientific texts for centuries. The episode also reveals how immigration policy shapes technological advantage: Bayezid II reportedly mocked Ferdinand of Spain for impoverishing his own kingdom while enriching the Ottoman Empire, a lesson in how exclusion exports innovation to rivals.
